title: Rousseau Turns on His Benefactor Hume
text:
In 1765 Jean-Jacques Rousseau was hounded out of France and Switzerland for his writings on religion. The Scottish philosopher David Hume, then the most celebrated British man of letters, offered to help. In January 1766 he brought Rousseau to England, found him a place to live, and quietly worked to obtain a pension for him from King George III.

Rousseau, already deeply suspicious by nature, came to believe the opposite of what was happening. A cruel joke made things worse: Horace Walpole wrote a mock letter from the King of Prussia ridiculing Rousseau, which circulated widely, and Rousseau suspected Hume was behind it. He grew convinced that Hume had brought him to England to dishonor him. In July 1766 he wrote Hume an enormous letter of accusation, listing every supposed sign of betrayal, including the way Hume had looked at him.

Hume was stunned and furious. Against the advice of some friends, he published his side of the correspondence as A Concise and Genuine Account of the Dispute. All of literary Europe took sides. Rousseau left England in 1767, and the two never reconciled.
lesson: Suspicion can twist even kindness into imagined betrayal. When you start reading every act as a plot against you, check your story before you act on it.
people: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, David Hume, Horace Walpole
source: David Hume, A Concise and Genuine Account of the Dispute between Mr. Hume and Mr. Rousseau (1766)
